title: Old Kingdom of Egypt
capsule: The Old Kingdom (c. 2700–2200 BCE) was the first great centralised state of ancient Egypt, spanning the Third through Sixth Dynasties, with its capital at Memphis. It is defined by the construction of the major pyramids: Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara (c. 2650 BCE), the Giza complex under Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure (c. 2575–2510 BCE), and dozens of provincial funerary monuments. The collapse of the Sixth Dynasty around 2181 BCE ushered in the First Intermediate Period, driven by a combination of administrative decentralisation, rising provincial power, and an extended drought documented in both textual and palaeoclimatic records.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core Nile Valley territory of the Old Kingdom is well established from archaeological and textual sources, though the precise extent of Egyptian influence into Nubia and the Levant varied by dynasty and is debated.
